title: Choral Response and 'I Say You Say'
author: Pritesh Raichura
summary: Pritesh Raichura distinguishes between two whole-class oral-response techniques teachers often conflate: 'I Say, You Say,' where the class repeats a single word or short phrase back to the teacher, and choral response, where the class chants an answer to a genuine question in unison after a countdown. He frames both as tools for securing 100% participation during an explanation, arguing that well-placed questions interrupt rather than break the flow of an explanation and are the key mechanism for sustaining pupil attention. Raichura evaluates each technique -- plus a third, checks for listening -- against three criteria he calls PAP: participation, accountability, and pace, showing that no single technique maximizes all three simultaneously. 'I Say, You Say' is high-participation but low-accountability and best used for vocabulary; choral response adds pace and some accountability signal through volume and mouth-movement; checks for listening sacrifice pace and participation for high individual accountability. He argues the techniques are only powerful when blended deliberately based on a read of the room -- firing choral questions when a class feels lethargic, switching to individual checks for listening when certain students appear to be coasting. The post positions this as 'phase 1' of a three-phase questioning model, with phases 2 and 3 addressed in companion posts.
points: Raichura's PAP framework (participation, accountability, pace) gives teachers a diagnostic lens for choosing among 'I Say You Say,' choral response, and checks for listening rather than treating them as interchangeable.

Choral response trades individual accountability for speed, letting teachers fire many questions in rapid succession and read confidence through response volume, whereas checks for listening sacrifice pace for high individual accountability.

The decision rule Raichura proposes -- deploy choral response when the room feels lethargic, switch to individual checks when specific students seem to be coasting -- turns technique selection into a live, situational judgment.
Both techniques are pitched as phase 1 tools for securing attention, explicitly separate from phase 2/3 techniques (turn-and-talk, mini-whiteboards) that probe genuine understanding.
quotes: The trick to sustaining attention is to ask pupils questions and to expect 100% participation DURING an explanation.
Questions interrupt the loss of attention. If done well, questions do not interrupt the flow of your explanation, as I once believed.
Choral response is NOT the same as 'I say, you say'. Choral response is about posing a question to the class which has a short answer, pausing and then saying: 'On 3… 1, 2, 3!'
It is far superior to mini-whiteboards because you can fire lots of questions in very little time.
As Claire Stoneman recently wrote about, we must refrain from using techniques for the sake of techniques.
It is only when BOTH strategies are used together, can you maximise all three of participation, accountability and pace (PAP)

If the class is feeling lethargic, fire choral response questions to increase participation and add pace. If it feels like some individuals are coasting, post a question, wait for hands up (or not!) and pick an individual that needs to be held to account for listening.
